home.story.title: How it works, in four steps
home.story.learn: the problem in brief, an interactive Earth-and-ridge experiment, and how RAVEN compares useful hours between sites.
home.story.horizon.title: The Earth stays close to the horizon
home.story.horizon.text: At the lunar south pole, Earth stays close to the horizon. Even when it is visible, a ridge can interrupt or weaken the radio link.
home.story.horizon.tech: Earth elevation from NASA/JPL DE440 ephemerides with Skyfield (D); libration moves it by about ±1° over the month. Terrain from PDS LOLA models (V).
home.story.earthAlt: The half-lit Earth rises above the Moon’s grey horizon in a black sky.
home.story.earthCredit: Earthrise over the lunar horizon, Apollo 8, 24 December 1968. NASA photograph, public domain.
home.story.ridge.title: Why a ridge matters
home.story.ridge.text: If the Earth is above the crest, the signal travels straight. If the crest just hides it, the signal does not switch off: it bends around the edge (diffraction) and arrives weaker.
home.story.ridge.tech: Fresnel-Kirchhoff knife-edge diffraction with ν = h·√(2/(λ·d₁)) (distant-source limit of ITU-R P.526-9, §4.1), plus the ITU-R P.526-9 rounded-ridge correction (formula verified, not measured); a Fresnel split-step table provides a comparison band (simulated, I). One dominant obstacle.
home.story.ridge.clear: Earth above the crest: the signal travels straight.
home.story.ridge.bent: The crest hides the Earth: the signal bends and arrives.
home.story.compute.title: What RAVEN calculates
home.story.compute.text: At each moment RAVEN checks sunlight, solar generation and battery charge, then evaluates the Earth link and Deep Space Network visibility. The result is useful operating hours, with each component visible.
home.story.compute.tech: Margin = C/N₀ − required (Eb/N₀) − 10·log₁₀ R − reserve margin; C/N₀ from power, dish gain η(πD/λ)², free-space loss (4πd/λ)², diffraction, the DSN station and Tsys. The same model as Simula, in the browser. Illustrative radio parameters (I).
home.story.compute.loading: The mini-simulator loads when you reach this section.
home.story.mission.title: Compare sites by useful hours
home.story.mission.text: Compare two sites across the chosen mission window. See when each can generate power, maintain a radio link and accumulate useful hours: seeing Earth alone does not mean a mission can operate.
home.story.mission.tech: Useful hours from hourly series: ephemeris elevation (D), LOLA profile along the Earth’s azimuth (V), geometric window versus link window (margin ≥ 0 dB), compensator. Here the elevation is synthetic (0.95° ± 0.55°), the ridge fixed (40 m at 2 km) and the data rate 1 Mbps.
home.story.mission.geo: Geometry only: Earth above the crest
home.story.mission.gained: extra hours in the transition zone
home.story.mission.summary: In an example month ({days} days), geometry alone gives {g} hours of contact; including the bent signal, the link closes for {r} hours.
home.story.mission.illustrative: Illustrative example, not a real site: for real sites use Sites and Analysis.
home.story.stack: FastAPI backend with Skyfield ephemerides and NASA/JPL kernels, LOLA DEM, ITU-R P.526-9 rounded-ridge correction with a Fresnel split-step comparison table; Svelte 5 frontend with uPlot charts and WebGL scenes with a 2D fallback. Sources: JPL IPN PR 42-226, Crane & Blood, ITU-R P.526.

trust.privacy.external.body: The server may download public scientific data from configured sources. Selecting an external profile or checkout link leaves RAVEN and is subject to that service's privacy practices. Optional third-party scripts, if configured, require their category consent.
trust.privacy.logs: HTTP hosting receives network information such as IP addresses and request headers. Application, web-server or proxy logs depend on the deployment. This prototype does not guarantee IP truncation, anonymisation or a particular retention period; the operator must document and configure these before launch.
trust.privacy.control: Use Dashboard to export or delete historical calculations and Mission Planner to manage saved configurations. Browser settings can clear site data. Consent preferences do not erase missions, stop necessary calculation requests or delete hosting logs.
trust.privacy.rights: A verified operator/privacy contact has not yet been published. Team placeholders and the learning assistant are not a channel for exercising privacy rights. trust.storage.backupTitle: Keeping a copy and deleting data
trust.storage.backup: Before clearing site data, download needed calculation JSON or print/save its report as PDF. Keep those files yourself: RAVEN has no automatic cloud backup, multi-device synchronisation or general import/restore of exported reports. Consent changes do not delete these records.

trust.terms.scope.title: Research and education
trust.terms.scope.body: RAVEN supports exploration, teaching and preliminary scenario comparison. It is not flight-qualified software, an operational mission forecast or a guarantee of power, communications or mission success.
trust.terms.evidence.title: Read the evidence, not only the result
trust.terms.evidence.body: Formula checks and implementation parity are not physical qualification. Panel, battery, soil and operational assumptions may be illustrative. Unknown terrain or samples remain unknown. Check the Model and Validation page, sources, parameters and version attached to every report.
trust.terms.commercial.title: Plans and purchases
trust.terms.commercial.body: Free, Premium and Enterprise describe a proposed offering. Prices are hypotheses and there is no implemented account/payment fulfilment or automatic licence activation. An external checkout link is not proof of entitlement. Approved seller details, billing, cancellation, refund and support terms are required before commercial launch.
trust.terms.data.title: Data and availability
trust.terms.data.body: Keep independent copies of reports you need. Browser archives can be cleared, blocked or lost; they are not backed up by a cloud account. Scientific data, network access or calculations can be unavailable. Do not submit sensitive data or rely on this prototype for safety-critical decisions.

analysis.comp.help: Rule: select the highest candidate rate whose predicted margin minus k·σ is at least 0 dB; if none qualifies, the link is not declared. An outage occurs when true margin plus noise N(0, σ) is below 0 dB. This is feed-forward control with a statistical margin, not reinforcement learning. σ = {sigma} dB and k are illustrative assumptions (tag I).

planner.intro: Select scenarios, calculate the mission and work through the six lessons. The scene uses the selected site and instant.
planner.sceneUnavailable: Terrain scene unavailable for this site or date. Timeline calculations do not require the DEM.
planner.lesson0: A crater and a massif can have different horizons. Formation centre coordinates are not necessarily landing sites.
planner.lesson1: The step determines time resolution: a transition can occur between samples. Change the parameters and calculate the mission.
planner.lesson2: The Sun is considered above the horizon when its upper limb clears the flat mask. Terrain may obscure it even when shown as visible here.
planner.lesson3: The model considers Earth's centre above the flat mask. A mountain can block it: the scene and RAVEN analysis examine terrain in more detail.
planner.lesson4: Visibility is not enough: the simplified link also requires a visible DSN station and sufficient margin. This timeline does not include diffraction.
planner.lesson5: Compare the fractions of sunlight, Earth and link. No single number decides the best site: the choice depends on mission requirements.
planner.unsynced: RAVEN samples unavailable or not synchronized: no terrain radio windows are shown.
planner.radioProgress: RAVEN calculation in progress; the DEM may take time.
planner.quizQuestion: If Earth is visible, is the link always available?
planner.quizCorrect: Correct: an available station and sufficient margin are also required; terrain may introduce further losses.
planner.quizIncorrect: Not necessarily: check the station, margin and terrain obstacles.

planner.quizSolarQuestion: Does the Sun above a flat horizon guarantee the terrain is illuminated?
planner.quizSolarCorrect: Correct: terrain may block sunlight, and the available DEM comparison is experimental.
planner.quizSolarIncorrect: No: the flat model excludes terrain shadows; the DEM comparison is experimental.
planner.quizMissingQuestion: When DEM data is missing, can we assume the line of sight is clear?
planner.quizMissingCorrect: Correct: terrain visibility is unknown, not guaranteed.
planner.quizMissingIncorrect: No: without DEM data terrain visibility is unknown.

planner.lunarDisclaimer: Results show potential under the stated assumptions, not a mission forecast. Limits: flat local horizon with elevation mask (no terrain: actual polar illumination depends on topography), no atmosphere or refraction, simplified link budget (free space, constant G/T, no verified coding gain). Illustrative parameters have no source.
planner.rfDisclaimer: Results show potential under the stated assumptions, not a mission forecast. Single dominant obstacle; no real South Pole radio measurements; regolith parameters from literature; rounded ridge correction from ITU-R P.526-9 clause 4.2 (formula checked against the text, not measured), with the difference from the simulated split-step shown as uncertainty. Parameters tagged I are illustrative and unsourced.
planner.sampling: Each sample is evaluated at the start of its step and represents [t, t + step); transitions are known only to the sampling resolution. Generation is evaluated at the start and battery state of charge at the end of each step. The model uses the LOLA terrain horizon.

antennaGuide.title: Which antenna should a mission use?
antennaGuide.intro: An antenna concentrates radio energy in particular directions. Choose it together with the required data rate, power, mounting space and ability to keep Earth inside its beam.
antennaGuide.omni: Useful for basic telemetry or uncertain vehicle orientation: broad coverage makes pointing less demanding. Lower gain leaves less link margin at the same power and data rate; reaching Earth may require a lower rate or more power.
antennaGuide.patch: An intermediate trade-off between size, gain and pointing. A compact directional antenna can suit a fixed lander when its mounting keeps Earth inside the beam; vehicle motion or lunar libration may require tracking.
antennaGuide.dish: Concentrates the signal for a larger margin or higher potential data rate. The narrower beam requires more accurate alignment, and possibly a gimbal, with added mass and complexity. High gain does not remove terrain blockage.
antennaGuide.station: DSN 18 m and 34 m refer to the receiving antenna on Earth, not the antenna on the lander. The larger receiver increases receiving gain; geometric visibility is not a booked DSN contact.
antennaGuide.model: RAVEN uses numerical gain, height, pointing and radio settings, not a qualified antenna catalogue. These are design trade-offs, not a hardware recommendation; verify beam pattern, polarization, coding, thermal limits and mounting with real mission data.
sitesLibrary.title: Sites library
sitesLibrary.intro: A general learning guide to lunar places: plains, valleys, massifs and polar craters. These descriptions do not depend on your mission dates, battery or radio results and do not rank landing suitability.
sitesLibrary.coordinates: A published coordinate can locate a feature centre rather than an intended landing point. A crater floor and its rim have different horizons; never treat a regional name as a precisely specified landing site.
sitesLibrary.apollo11: An equatorial near-side landing reference in the Sea of Tranquillity. Use it to understand how low-latitude geometry differs from the near-horizon Sun and Earth directions at the lunar poles.
sitesLibrary.apollo17: A near-side highland valley landing reference at Taurus-Littrow. Valleys illustrate why nearby mountains and the local horizon matter even when a body's elevation is above the horizontal.
sitesLibrary.massif: A south-polar massif: elevated terrain can offer a different horizon from nearby depressions. Elevation alone guarantees neither uninterrupted sunlight nor a clear path to Earth.
sitesLibrary.crater: A south-polar crater reference. The floor, walls and rim are distinct topographic settings; terrain can hide the Sun or Earth differently at each location.
sitesLibrary.shackleton: A crater very close to the south pole. Distinguish its floor from nearby peaks: a named bright ridge does not mean the crater centre is permanently illuminated. Longitude also becomes less informative near the pole.
sitesLibrary.generic: A catalogue location for studying lunar geometry. Its name and coordinate are not evidence of mission feasibility.
sitesLibrary.featureCentre: Coordinate basis: centre of the named feature, not a published landing-region centre.
disclosure.title: Independence, SI contributions and sources
disclosure.affiliation: Not affiliated with NASA. RAVEN is an independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA, the governments of Russia or China, or their space agencies. Using public data, publications or agency names does not imply sponsorship or approval.
disclosure.terminology: This site uses SI — Super intelligence — for automated development assistance. Executive Order 14434 of 29 September 2026 directs this terminology within the US federal executive branch; RAVEN adopts it voluntarily, not as a federal agency or as a claim that the order binds this independent site. The label does not certify superhuman capabilities. Historical publication titles, source quotations and software/provider identifiers retain their original names.

disclosure.contributionsTitle: How SI contributed to this web app
disclosure.contributions: GitHub Copilot-assisted development contributed to frontend/backend implementation and debugging, bilingual interface and lesson drafting, research-source inspection, automated tests, numerical consistency checks, installer/CI fixes and local deployment checks. SI helped write and inspect code and documentation; it did not supply lunar measurements or independent experimental validation.
disclosure.responsibility: The authors remain responsible for requirements, source review, code acceptance and scientific interpretation. Mission results come from the deterministic RAVEN engine and its declared inputs, not conversational SI answers. Passing software tests or agreeing with another model does not qualify real mission hardware.
disclosure.legend: Data sources provide inputs; publications describe methods; reference comparisons check specific calculations. V means a sourced value, D a derived value and I an illustrative assumption. These tags do not mean that a whole model stage is verified.
disclosure.validation: The references below support the indicated parts of the project, not a blanket claim of validation. Current check status, tolerances, limitations and reproduction procedures are listed on Model and validation; S2/S3 and real hardware retain their declared evidence gaps.
disclosure.evidenceLink: Read current validation evidence and reproduction details
disclosure.source.de440: S1 — Planetary/lunar ephemeris model underlying the DE440s kernel. The paper is a method/data reference, not a validation of the complete planner.
disclosure.source.spice: S1 — Credit for NAIF/SPICE ancillary geometry data and kernel conventions.
disclosure.source.horizons: S1 — Independent reference service used for specific Sun/Earth geometry comparisons documented in the validation evidence.
disclosure.source.lola: S2 — Source of lunar elevation products used to construct terrain profiles and horizons. Sourced terrain does not establish the accuracy of every local horizon calculation.
disclosure.source.illumination: S2/S3 — Published horizon-based illumination method. Comparisons against NASA derived illumination products are model comparisons, not independent instantaneous measurements.
disclosure.source.gazetteer: S0 — Coordinate provenance for named lunar features. A feature centre is not necessarily a published landing-region centre.
disclosure.source.diffraction: S5 — Knife-edge and rounded-obstacle diffraction equations. Checking implementation of a recommendation is not a lunar RF measurement.
disclosure.source.dsn: S5 — Referenced X-band receiving gain and system-noise parameters for 34 m BWG stations; does not establish station scheduling.
disclosure.source.lander: S4/S5 — Reference-design examples for communications power conversion and service margin. The hardware defaults used here remain illustrative where tagged I.
disclosure.source.power: S4 — Literature source for solar-cell efficiency examples. It does not validate this site's battery, thermal or dust assumptions.
disclosure.source.solarMap: S3 — Derived multi-year illumination maps used for explicitly limited plausibility comparisons. They are not instantaneous measurements or an independent validation of our solar-disc integration.
disclosure.source.dsnCoordinates: S6 — Published Earth-station coordinates used for geometric visibility checks. Neither the coordinates nor the calculation provide an operational reservation.
disclosure.source.surveyor: S5 — Historical published reference for specific radio-budget arithmetic checks. Reproducing that reference does not measure or qualify a south-polar RAVEN mission.
disclosure.source.surface: S5 — Published lunar radar reference for specific surface/reflectivity comparisons documented in the evidence. This is not validation of every multipath, roughness or antenna assumption.

planner.missionTitle: Coupled mission timeline: Sun, battery, radio and DSN
planner.missionIntroLearning: One calculation per step for the site shown: how much of the Sun the terrain lets through, how much power the panel makes, how the battery charges and drains, whether the radio link closes at the chosen bit rate and whether a 34 m DSN antenna sees the Moon. A step is useful only when the rover has power AND the link closes AND the DSN sees it. Unknown data is shown in grey and never counted as useful.
planner.missionIntroAdvanced: Per step: visible solar-disc fraction from the 200 km LOLA horizon mask → array power (illustrative panel, tag I) → battery with active, comms-only and survival loads (tag I) → RAVEN RF margin at the chosen rate (single dominant ridge, ITU-R P.526-9 cylinder term) → geometric visibility of the 34 m DSN complexes (unknown for the 18 m class). useful = operational AND margin ≥ 0 AND DSN visible. An unknown input makes that step and the later battery history unknown. Potential under stated assumptions, not a forecast.

model.learn: The eight steps of the RAVEN model, and how far each one has been checked against independent evidence.
model.intro: RAVEN is one chain of eight stages (S0 to S7) that reads one parameter registry. This page is built live from the validation matrix of the server: if the server is not reachable, nothing is shown instead of an invented table. No row is a radio or power measurement on the Moon.

model.pipeline.title: The pipeline
model.pipeline.intro: Each stage reads the outputs of earlier ones. Select a stage to open its evidence.
model.stage.s0.name: Time and site
model.stage.s0.what: Fixes the time grid and the site: coordinates, height, scenario limits.
model.stage.s0.plain: Sets when and where we look: the instants, the site and its coordinates.

model.stage.s1.what: Sun, Earth and Moon directions and distances from the site at each instant (JPL DE440).
model.stage.s1.plain: Where the Sun and the Earth are in the sky of the site, instant by instant.
model.stage.s2.name: Terrain
model.stage.s2.what: Horizon mask from real LOLA elevation data, and the ridge that blocks the Earth direction.
model.stage.s2.plain: Which hills hide the Sun or the Earth, from real lunar elevation data.
model.stage.s3.name: Illumination
model.stage.s3.what: Visible fraction of the solar disc over the horizon mask.
model.stage.s3.plain: How much of the Sun is actually above the local horizon.
model.stage.s4.name: Power and battery
model.stage.s4.what: Energy balance of an illustrative panel, loads and battery.
model.stage.s4.plain: Whether an illustrative lander keeps its battery charged.
model.stage.s5.name: RF link
model.stage.s5.what: Link budget: free-space loss, knife-edge and rounded-ridge diffraction, antenna, margin.
model.stage.s5.plain: Whether the radio signal survives the grazing path over the ridge, and by how many dB.
model.stage.s6.name: DSN
model.stage.s6.what: Geometric visibility of the Moon from the three Deep Space Network complexes.
model.stage.s6.plain: When a big ground antenna on Earth can see the Moon at all.
model.stage.s7.name: Mission rules
model.stage.s7.what: Definitions of usable hours, windows and the ranking of sites.
model.stage.s7.plain: How the earlier results are combined into hours you can use and a ranking of sites.
model.stage.time.name: Window edges
model.stage.time.what: Refinement of window edges by bisection.
model.stage.time.plain: How precisely the start and end times of each window are found.

roadmap.title: A transparent roadmap for a research prototype.
roadmap.intro: These are possible improvements, not promises of operational capability. Each item stays linked to a model stage, an estimated effort and the evidence or decision it still needs.
roadmap.currentText: The single RAVEN engine, custom sites and the educational workflow are implemented. Validation gaps remain visible rather than being hidden behind a product label.

roadmap.table.caption: Future improvements, estimated effort and current blockers
roadmap.item.1.name: Independent RF validation
roadmap.item.1.summary: Reproduce a complete lunar link budget against an independent published reference.
roadmap.item.1.blocker: No complete public reference budget with all antenna, coding and loss terms.
roadmap.item.2.name: Rounded-ridge arbiter
roadmap.item.2.summary: Resolve the difference between the ITU rounded-ridge approximation and a converged wave model.
roadmap.item.2.blocker: No agreed independent arbiter or convergence result for the reference geometry.

about.title: A clearer way to reason about a lunar link.
about.intro: RAVEN is a mission-planning and learning prototype for a lander near the lunar south pole, where the Earth can sit close to the horizon and terrain changes the conversation.
about.problem.title: The problem
about.problem.text: Near the south pole, a site can have sunlight, an Earth line of sight, a usable radio path and a reachable ground station at different times. A flat horizon or a single optimistic score hides those trade-offs.
about.does.title: What RAVEN does
about.does.text: RAVEN lets you explore sites, dates and assumptions through one traceable workflow.
about.does.1: Computes Sun, Earth and DSN geometry over time.
about.does.2: Uses LOLA terrain where coverage and download limits allow it, and keeps missing terrain explicitly unknown.
about.does.3: Shows energy, radio, terrain and validation status without presenting a prototype as flight-qualified software.
about.model.title: One model, not several hidden calculators
about.model.text: The RAVEN engine is a chain of stages. Pages are views of the same server-side results; the browser mirror is limited to the closed-form S5 link calculation and is checked with fixtures.
about.model.s0: site context, coordinates and declared inputs.
about.model.s5: radio propagation, diffraction and link margin.
about.data.title: Data and sources
about.data.text: Inputs are tagged as sourced, derived or illustrative. Their provenance remains visible in exported results.
about.data.1: JPL NAIF / DE440-based ephemerides for Sun, Earth and Moon geometry.
about.data.2: NASA LOLA / PDS elevation products, selected and cached on demand for custom sites.
about.data.3: DSN documentation, NASA technical reports and ITU-R P.526 references for independent checks and method context.
about.validation.title: What is validated
about.validation.text: Geometry, selected formulae, DSN coordinates and several numerical invariants have independent checks. The project also records differential NASA comparisons and real-engine custom-site regressions.
about.validation.notice: A validation entry is not a flight qualification. Absolute lunar link margin, rounded-ridge diffraction, multipath, energy hardware and operational DSN scheduling remain open.
about.limits.title: Limits we keep visible
about.limits.text: Terrain resolution and range depend on the product and download cap. Unknown terrain propagates to horizon and RF results. Illustrative parameters, sampled windows, missing atmospheric effects and the absence of mission operations data all limit interpretation.
about.history.title: From GrazingLink to RAVEN
about.history.text: The project began as GrazingLink, a research investigation of a grazing lunar-to-Earth radio path. RAVEN keeps that research lineage while turning it into a single, explainable interface for exploration, comparison and learning.
about.team.title: Team and contact
about.team.text: The public team and legal details are intentionally kept as placeholders until the project owner provides the official names, roles and contact information.
about.license.title: Licence
about.license.text: The project code is distributed under Apache-2.0. Third-party assets and dependencies are listed on the Licences page; scientific sources are cited in the repository documentation.

journey.title: Build your lunar mission
journey.missionIntro: One decision at a time. Choose your comparison and what matters to your study. All hardware settings are illustrative, not flight configurations.
journey.sitesIntro: Assign a catalogue site to A or B, or pick your own coordinates on the lunar globe. The map is illustrative; terrain availability is checked separately.
journey.periodIntro: Choose when and for how long. Both scenarios use the same duration, resolution and hardware assumptions.
journey.energyIntro: Configure how the lander collects sunlight. Power and battery results will come from the same RAVEN evaluation as the radio assessment.
journey.radioIntro: Start with a preset, then adjust the antenna and data rate. Optional visual tools explain terrain and propagation without leaving this journey.
journey.compareIntro: Evaluate both scenarios together. Inspect the same sampled instant across the timeline and charts, then prepare your report.
journey.reportIntro: Review the complete document before exporting. Unknown data and illustrative assumptions remain explicit in every export.
journey.reliabilityIntro: Declare the components and assumptions for the optional reliability study. Results appear here after the comparison has been calculated; nothing is assumed by default.
journey.reliabilityPending: Reliability results need a current comparison. Calculate it in the Compare step, then return here to read the charts, margins and statistics.
journey.reliabilityPointer: Reliability inputs, thermal and radiation margins have their own step.

journey.terrainNote: Coverage is not a guarantee of cached data. Custom sites may require a small download, only after an estimate and your explicit confirmation. Unknown terrain is never replaced with a flat horizon.
journey.customInvalid: Enter a valid site name (letters, numbers, spaces and simple punctuation; up to 40 characters).
journey.stepAuto: For {days} days the interval was raised to {step} min so the period stays within 1,500 samples per scenario. Larger intervals remain available.
journey.sampleCount: {count} samples per scenario; maximum {max}. Increase the interval or shorten the duration if necessary.
journey.periodNote: Times are UTC, not your browser's local time. Events between samples are not all resolved; a shorter sampling interval is not a claim of greater physical accuracy.
journey.panelIllustration: Orientation illustration only, not a computed lighting simulation.
journey.efficiencyHint: Fraction of incident solar energy converted to electricity: 0.30 means 30%.
journey.energyDefaultNote: Battery capacity, loads and efficiencies use the model's declared illustrative defaults. The report includes the actual values used by the server.
journey.bitrateHint: A higher data rate requires more radio margin. DSN visibility is geometric only: no station booking or availability is implied. The 18 m option is illustrative.
journey.sceneNote: This scene explains the selected site and instant. It is not the final mission evaluation and does not include every correction or energy assumption.

journey.waveNote: Educational propagation experiment with its own stated parameters, not a prediction for the chosen site. Changing this experiment does not change your mission configuration or report.
journey.computing: Evaluating Sun, terrain, energy, radio and DSN with RAVEN engine. A terrain-download confirmation may appear.
journey.cancelled: Calculation cancelled. Previous results, if any, have been kept.
journey.downloadDeclined: The required terrain download was declined. No mission result was generated; confirm the download or select another site.
journey.terrainCap: The required terrain exceeds the download limits. Select another site or inspect terrain availability.
journey.stale: Configuration changed. These are the previous calculation's results, not the current draft. Recalculate before generating the report.
journey.calculateFirst: Complete the previous steps and simulate the mission before generating a report.
journey.honesty: Potential under stated assumptions, not a mission forecast. Unknown does not mean impossible.
journey.powerZeroDark: Solar power chart omitted: the Sun is below the horizon for the whole window, so generation is 0 W throughout (a real zero, not an unknown).
journey.powerZero: Solar power chart omitted: generation is 0 W throughout the window (a real zero, not an unknown).
stats.energyAllZero: Energy comparison omitted: harvested and unmet energy are both 0 Wh in every compared scenario (real zeros, not unknowns).
journey.measuresCaption: Known and unknown hours, side by side
journey.measuresNote: These are two different measures, not to be added. RF availability is unknown where the terrain is not modelled. The mission state is unknown over a longer period because it also depends on the battery, which cannot be followed after the first step with unknown radio load.
journey.samplingNote: Sampling: {step} min. Percentages are unknown if any relevant sample is unknown. Battery charge is evaluated at the end of each step.

journey.replayNote: Replay follows the sampled timeline independently of optional 3D rendering. Pause replay before selecting an exact instant.

rel.title: Mission reliability, degradation and protection
rel.scope: Preliminary RAVEN engine arithmetic from declared assumptions (tag I), not measured mission reliability or hardware qualification. No missing rate is treated as zero.
rel.conditions: All listed components are critical and independent in a series chain. Redundancy, common-cause failures and unlisted hardware are not assessed. Conditional operating probabilities assume thermal and radiation requirements hold; missing or exceeded margins invalidate that interpretation, not prove certain failure.
rel.example: Load illustrative assumptions — not real hardware
rel.exampleBasis: Illustrative demonstration only: synthetic rates, shock probabilities, temperatures, shielding and tolerances. Not measured lunar conditions or qualified hardware data.
rel.noDefaults: Start with unknown values, or explicitly load the demonstration. Replace its assumptions with component datasheets, environmental analyses and test evidence.
rel.fractions: Probabilities, losses, thresholds and transmission are fractions from 0 to 1, not percentages. Vehicle phase probabilities exclude separately entered component shock failures, to avoid double counting.
rel.applyPower: Add the declared continuous thermal-control load to the energy calculation
rel.powerScope: Optional incremental demand, added to both survival and active loads in the existing RAVEN energy model. Base loads already include illustrative heating: enter only additional demand, not the same heaters twice. Changing this option requires a new simulation. No thermostat duty cycle or cooler COP is inferred.
rel.invalidPower: Declare a valid additional thermal load; resulting survival and active loads must remain inside the engine's bounds.
rel.invalid: Check the reliability inputs, temperature intervals and assumption source. Recovery time is zero or at least 0.000001 h.
rel.error: The reliability calculation failed. Results are unavailable; retry the calculation.
rel.busy: RAVEN engine is calculating the reliability study…
rel.protectionTitle: Protect electronics before interpreting a survival estimate
rel.thermalHelp: Cold: consider insulation/MLI, thermal isolation, survival heaters and controlled warm-up. Heat: consider sunshields, suitable optical coatings, radiators, heat paths and active regulation where justified. Enter predicted component/junction temperature extremes AFTER protection across launch, cruise, landing and surface operations, plus tested operating limits. Selecting a protection type does not calculate temperatures, mass or qualification; thermal balance and thermal-vacuum tests remain necessary.
rel.radiationHelp: Use mission-specific dose analysis and radiation-tested components. Shielding, rad-tolerant parts, ECC, watchdogs, latch-up protection and safe recovery may reduce different risks, not eliminate them. Dose = declared krad(Si)/h × shield transmission × (cruise + sampled surface hours). No shielding thickness/particle transport is inferred; TID, displacement damage and single-event effects are distinct. Upset/restart rates require a separate justified assumption.
rel.field.dose_rate_krad_h: Unshielded TID dose rate in silicon
rel.survival: Hardware survival at end of sampled window
rel.operational: Conditional operational probability at window end
rel.usefulBounds: Useful-hour lower / upper bound with unknown samples
rel.durationScope: Unavailable hours include loss before landing, irreversible faults, recoverable outages and performance exhaustion; this is not the duration of a single fault. Useful hours integrate equipment availability over known engine resource windows; unknown windows remain bounds. The unsampled remainder of the requested period is excluded. No random event history or exact failure date is predicted.
rel.faultTable: Fault and restart statistics — declared full exposure
rel.environment.within_declared_envelope: Inside declared temperature/TID envelope — not independently verified
rel.environment.outside_declared_envelop: WARNING: declared temperature or TID limit exceeded; conditional reliability is not a mission-success estimate
rel.cutoff: Minimum usable performance is crossed after {hours} from landing
rel.incomplete: Incomplete assumptions: a chain probability or duration cannot be calculated. Partial component checks remain visible.
rel.chartScope: Analytic conditional statistics, not a sampled failure trajectory or confidence interval. Performance is an aggregate proxy; RF gain, solar efficiency and battery capacity are not time-derated by this curve.
rel.chart.title: Reliability, thermal and radiation comparisons
rel.chart.comparisonScope: A and B use common axes within each chart. Both scenarios share the declared component/protection assumptions: identical curves do not prove that the sites have the same real environment. Exact values and missing data remain visible; use the numerical tables for very small differences.
rel.chart.elapsed: Hours since landing, not calendar UTC. Solid A / dashed B; legend values are at each scenario's own end. Missing samples break the line.
rel.chart.chainScope: Cumulative probabilities, not independent per-phase success rates. Surface operation remains conditional on performance and environmental requirements.
rel.chart.faultScope: Launch/landing shocks plus absorbing surface faults, including unsuccessful recovery. The scale adapts to show small probabilities; it is not always 0–100%.
rel.identical: Scenarios A and B give identical figures here because the declared assumptions are shared (same components, rates, environment and duration). One series and one table are shown, labelled A = B. This coincidence does not validate that the two environments are equal.
rel.chart.sharedScope: The declared mean recovery duration is shared by A and B. It is not a predicted incident duration or total mission downtime; zero means explicitly assumed instantaneous recovery.
rel.chart.retention: Component performance: landing and surface end
rel.chart.retentionScope: Shared landing retention versus each scenario's final retention. Aggregate declared degradation, not a qualified RF, battery or solar ageing law.
rel.chart.thermalScope: Shared worst hot/cold margin across all mission phases, not a temperature history. Zero is the declared limit; negative, hatched bars exceed it. No thermal solver is run.
rel.chart.radiation: Shielded dose versus declared TID tolerance
rel.chart.radiationScope: A/B doses include cruise and sampled surface exposure. Compare each component with its own tolerance bar. Different component tolerances are not interchangeable; this is linear TID arithmetic, not particle transport or a single-event prediction.
rel.chart.hoursScope: Absolute expected hours for each sampled duration. Useful lower/upper bounds bracket unknown resource windows; they are not extra hours to add to availability. No exact useful estimate is implied when the bounds differ.
stats.partitionScope: A complete partition of sampled engine hours, not a success probability. Unknown time is neither useful nor confirmed failure. Known non-useful hours may be limited by energy, RF or DSN, not a hardware fault. The unsampled remainder is excluded.
stats.noPartition: No complete positive total: proportions are not drawn. Missing or inconsistent values are not normalised to 100%.
stats.energyScope: Harvested energy and unmet demand are separate measures, not parts of a pie or a complete energy balance. Engine totals may cover only a known prefix; missing totals remain unknown. Check the coverage notices and SoC curves.
stats.costScope: Same-currency/base-year user estimates plus the engine's declared contingency amount. Missing items remain unknown; shown categories need not be the full mission cost. Funding is not a cost category. This is not a quotation or feasibility finding.
stats.carbonScope: Declared phase emissions, not measured footprint or an independently verified LCA/ESG assessment. Unknown phases are not zero; partial values are not normalised into percentages of a complete footprint.
rel.formula: Model: permanent hazard h = λ + ν(1 − r); recoverable rate k = νr; recovery μ = 1/mean duration. Independent up/down availability is combined with phase survival and exponential degradation; useful-hour integrals use the engine's known resource windows.
journey.librarySaved: Mission saved in your browser library.
journey.instantPreviewNote: Optional one-sample preview from RAVEN engine. It does not evaluate the whole mission or predict battery endurance. Changing a parameter invalidates the preview.
journey.kEffect: k changes the bitrate selected by the statistical compensator, not the physical margin at a fixed bitrate. Higher k is more conservative. Unknown terrain leaves this selection unknown.
journey.partialEnergy: Battery minimum and harvested energy cover only the known prefix, up to the first unknown input. Confirmed useful hours do not establish feasibility over the missing interval.
journey.batteryFull: The battery stays at its capacity ceiling (100%). Generated energy is cumulative panel output, not additional stored charge. Generation above the loads cannot raise charge beyond 100%.
journey.noFiniteRfMargin: RF is classified closed by the model's terrain constraints. No finite dB margin is supplied for these steps; this is not a failed calculation.
journey.noSupportedRate: No supported transmission rate for the sampled closed RF links; no rate curve is expected.
journey.unregisteredParameter: No matching parameter-registry entry; the server value is shown, not an unknown calculation.
journey.noSunWindow: No sampled sunlight reaches this site according to the terrain horizon during this period. Zero solar generation is a known model result, not missing data.
journey.batteryOnly: With no solar generation, the mission draws on its initial battery reserve. Useful operation can continue in shadow until the energy policy limits it.
journey.energyPrefix: Battery minimum and harvested-energy totals cover only the first {known} of {total} hours, up to {end}. Later battery states are unknown, not zero; this is not a complete energy result.
journey.energyUnknownRf: RF availability is outside the model at the first unknown battery step. The transmission load cannot be determined, so the battery calculation cannot continue without an assumed load.
journey.rfUnknownCoverage: RF availability is unknown for {hours} of {total} hours. Unknown is not a failed link; no RF percentage can be established for the complete period.
history.title: Saved calculations
history.intro: Local to this browser, without account sync. Only final calculations are saved, never previews. Up to {limit} snapshots and 2 million text characters (about 4 MB); no automatic deletion when full.
history.confirmClear: I confirm deleting the entire local calculation history
history.empty: No archived calculations. New final calculations are saved automatically.
history.snapshot: Read-only historical snapshot, with its original inputs and model identity. Selecting it does not change the Planner draft or prepare a current report.
history.oldModel: Saved model: {saved}; current model: {current}. These historical numbers have not been recalculated with the current implementation.
history.incompatible: This saved calculation is invalid or incompatible with the current parameter registry. It has not been replaced or interpreted as a current result. You can delete it explicitly.
history.readError: Calculation history is unreadable or browser storage is unavailable. Existing data has not been overwritten. To reset it, confirm clearing the history.
history.writeError: The calculation could not be saved to local history: browser storage is unavailable or its quota is exhausted. Previous snapshots are preserved; the current result remains available in this tab.
history.full: Calculation history is full. Delete a saved calculation in Dashboard before saving another; previous snapshots have not been evicted.
history.tooLarge: This calculation exceeds the remaining history size limit. Download its JSON or remove previous snapshots in Dashboard. No saved calculation has been deleted.
history.invalid: The calculation could not be archived because its inputs, samples or model identity failed validation.
history.saved: Final calculation saved in local history.
history.deleted: Selected history data deleted. The latest calculation in this tab and the Planner draft are unchanged.
lessons.title: Lunar planning, step by step
lessons.intro: Start from zero: seven lessons follow the Mission Planner, then eight explain engine stages S0–S7. Read one card, try its quiz and review the explanation before continuing. Progress lasts for this visit; these lessons do not run a second scientific engine.
course.toolNote: Optional practice opens in a new tab, keeping this lesson and its progress open. A report requires a completed Planner calculation. Progress lasts for this visit.
course.mission.title: Mission: define the goal
course.mission.body: A mission needs energy to operate and a radio path to send data. Give the study a name, choose a priority and set minimum sunlight or RF availability requirements. These thresholds express your goal; they do not improve the physical conditions.
course.mission.example: A 50% RF requirement asks for communication during at least half the evaluated period. It does not create a radio window.
course.mission.question: What does changing the minimum RF requirement do?
course.mission.b: It changes the requirement used to assess the result.
course.mission.explanation: Requirements are decision criteria. Change the hardware, site or period to change the calculated physical result; changing a target alone cannot improve it.
course.sites.title: Sites: choose the locations
course.sites.body: Compare two sites during one period, or one site at two dates. Assign A and B using the map or catalogue. The Sites library describes terrain types independently of the mission. Check the coordinate source and whether it identifies a point or a feature centre.
course.sites.example: Haworth's catalogue coordinate is the crater centre. A landing point on its rim would be a different location with a different horizon.
course.sites.question: Does a crater-centre coordinate describe every point on its rim?
course.sites.a: Yes, every point has the same horizon.
course.sites.b: No, the rim requires its own location and terrain analysis.
course.sites.c: Yes, if the coordinate has a verified source.
course.sites.explanation: A sourced coordinate is not a verified landing recommendation. Relief varies locally, and a named region may not have a publicly specified landing centre.
course.period.title: Period: time and sampling
course.period.body: Set the start in UTC, duration in days and sampling step in minutes. Both start and end must fit the ephemeris interval. The engine evaluates conditions at sampled instants; a coarse step can miss short windows and approximate energy transitions poorly.
course.period.example: Seven days at 60 minutes gives 168 steps; at 1,440 minutes it gives seven daily steps, not continuous observation.
course.period.question: Which setting better resolves a brief shadow transition?
course.period.a: A shorter sampling step, within the point limit.
course.period.explanation: Finer sampling improves temporal resolution, not physical qualification. The point cap still applies; compare resolutions when a decision depends on a narrow event.
course.energy.title: Energy: panel and battery
course.energy.body: Panel area, cell efficiency and orientation determine electrical power in watts (W). Tracking follows the Sun ideally; a horizontal panel receives little at grazing angles. Battery capacity is energy in watt-hours (Wh), while SOC is its stored fraction. Loads and conversion losses drain it.
course.energy.example: A panel delivering 100 W for two hours generates 200 Wh before storage losses. A 100% battery cannot store unlimited surplus.
course.energy.question: How much energy does 100 W sustained for two hours produce?
course.energy.explanation: Energy equals power multiplied by time. W and Wh are different quantities; generated energy is not necessarily energy retained in the battery.
course.radio.title: Communications: rate and antenna
course.radio.body: Choose bits per second, lander antenna gain and height, receiving station and uncertainty factor k. Gain concentrates the beam rather than creating transmitter power. Low-gain antennas favour coverage; high-gain antennas favour margin but demand accurate pointing. Read the antenna guide before choosing numerical settings.
course.radio.example: A high-gain dish can improve a link when aligned, but a vehicle that cannot keep Earth inside its narrow beam may lose that benefit.
course.radio.question: What must accompany a high-gain antenna choice?
course.radio.a: The assumption that terrain no longer matters.
course.radio.b: The assumption that no power is needed.
course.radio.c: A compatible pointing and mounting design.
course.radio.explanation: Gain, beam width, pointing, mass and power form a trade-off. DSN diameter describes the Earth receiver, not the lander's antenna; RAVEN does not qualify specific hardware.
course.simulation.title: Simulation: read the graphs
course.simulation.body: Calculate the two scenarios, choose A or B and move through the timeline. Sun/Earth curves show centre elevation; power shows generation; SOC shows charge at step end; RF margin and selected rate show communication conditions. The 3D scene illustrates the selected data, not an independent measurement.
course.simulation.example: A flat 100% SOC can mean charging exceeds consumption and surplus is curtailed. A gap means unavailable data, not a flat zero.
course.simulation.question: A battery curve contains a gap. How should you read it?
course.simulation.explanation: Read the units and unknown-coverage notes. Do not interpolate a missing scientific result just to make a smoother graph.
course.report.title: Report: justify a decision
course.report.body: The eighth Planner step exports the report. First use the Mission dossier step to supply mission goals, user cost assumptions and ESG context; RAVEN engine totals are arithmetic on your estimates. Optional RAVEN SI produces labeled, unreviewed proposals, not evidence. Inspect useful hours, availability, energy, unknown coverage and window tables; compare requirements and record your reasoning. Sources and illustrative parameters remain attached; useful time is not proof of whole-mission survival.
course.report.example: A mission may accumulate useful hours and later exhaust its battery. Large generated-energy totals do not by themselves establish uninterrupted operation.
course.report.question: What should accompany a site recommendation?
course.report.b: A claim that every model is physically validated.
course.report.c: Requirements, assumptions, unknown intervals and supporting evidence.
course.report.explanation: The report documents potential under stated assumptions. A result that meets a percentage threshold can still have blackouts or missing intervals.
course.s0.title: S0 — Context and inputs
course.s0.body: S0 resolves the site and coordinate provenance, validates UTC, units and parameter bounds, and builds the time grid. The registry distinguishes sourced values (V), derived values (D) and illustrative assumptions (I). Valid input is necessary, but is not a physically validated mission.
course.s0.example: An illustrative battery capacity is a configurable hypothesis, even when the arithmetic using it is correct.
course.s0.question: What does an I tag mean?
course.s0.a: An illustrative assumption, not a measurement.
course.s0.c: An invalid result in every case.
course.s0.explanation: Provenance tags describe where inputs come from. They are distinct from a model stage's validation status and from whether a sample is known.
course.s1.title: S1 — Ephemeris geometry
course.s1.body: NASA/JPL DE440 kernels and lunar orientation provide Sun/Earth directions and distances at each UTC instant. Azimuth is a horizontal direction; elevation is the body's centre above the local horizontal in degrees. Geometry alone does not include terrain blockage.
course.s1.example: A Sun centre at +0.5° may still be hidden behind a ridge higher than that direction. The finite solar disc also matters.
course.s1.question: Does positive Sun elevation guarantee illumination?
course.s1.b: No, compare the disc with the terrain horizon.
course.s1.c: No, the Sun must be at the zenith.
course.s1.explanation: The horizontal and terrain horizon are different references. Likewise, a negative Earth elevation is not automatically blockage if the visible terrain horizon lies even lower.
course.s2.title: S2 — Terrain and horizon
course.s2.body: LOLA elevation data describe the lunar surface. The engine samples profiles, includes curvature and observer height, and finds the terrain horizon in each direction. The radio profile and more distant terrain have declared limits; missing coverage is not silently replaced with a flat surface.
course.s2.example: Raising an antenna changes its local view, but does not supply a missing terrain tile or validate the terrain model.
course.s2.question: How should missing terrain coverage be handled?
course.s2.explanation: Unknown terrain cannot justify a visibility or radio margin. Coordinate sourcing, DEM processing checks and full physical validation are separate evidence levels.
course.s3.title: S3 — Solar illumination
course.s3.body: S3 compares the finite solar disc with the direction-dependent terrain horizon, not just one centre elevation. Its visible-disc fraction ranges from zero to one. Any positive fraction counts as a lit sample, while power still scales with the visible fraction and panel incidence.
course.s3.example: A tiny visible solar sliver can make a sample lit while generating very little electricity.
course.s3.question: Does 100% sampled sunlight mean full panel power throughout?
course.s3.a: Yes, sunlight percentage is panel power.
course.s3.b: No, disc fraction and orientation still matter.
course.s3.c: Yes, unless the battery is empty.
course.s3.explanation: Sunlight percentage counts lit samples. It is neither a full-disc percentage nor an electrical efficiency measurement; sampling can miss events between instants.
course.s4.title: S4 — Power and stored energy
course.s4.body: S4 applies distance, incidence, panel efficiency and solar visibility to generation, then integrates battery charging and loads with losses and reserve rules. An unknown required input stops the known battery trajectory; later SOC cannot be recovered merely because a later RF sample becomes known.
course.s4.example: If only the first 24 hours are known, an 87.4% minimum SOC describes that prefix, not the rest of a year.
course.s4.question: Can a known-prefix minimum establish full-period endurance?
course.s4.b: Yes, if the final graph has gaps.
course.s4.c: No, later battery states remain unknown.
course.s4.explanation: Generation can be known separately from battery state. Prefix-scoped totals and minimum SOC must not be presented as a complete energy result; zero and unknown differ.
course.s5.title: S5 — RF budget and compensator
course.s5.body: The radio budget combines transmitter power/gain, receiver gain/noise, distance loss, terrain diffraction and declared corrections. It computes margin at the configured bit rate. The compensator uses uncertainty k to choose a supported rate conservatively; this is potential capacity, not measured throughput.
course.s5.example: At unchanged power, gains and losses, multiplying bit rate by ten reduces margin by 10 dB. A physical 0 dB closure can still miss a 3 dB service requirement.
course.s5.question: What does a tenfold bit-rate increase do to the same budget?
course.s5.explanation: Margin subtracts 10·log10(bit rate). Uncertainty adjustment changes the selected rate, not the physical margin at a fixed rate. Unsupported RF conditions remain unknown.
course.s6.title: S6 — DSN geometric overlap
course.s6.body: S6 checks whether the Moon is above the selected elevation mask at Earth receiving locations. Communication requires overlap between a usable lander link and a visible receiver. This geometric calculation does not include DSN booking, weather, operations or guaranteed station access.
course.s6.example: A receiver that can geometrically see the Moon may already be allocated to another spacecraft.
course.s6.question: Does a geometric DSN window guarantee an allocated contact?
course.s6.a: No, scheduling and operations are not modelled.
course.s6.explanation: The engine establishes geometric potential only. Station availability for an actual mission requires a separate operational agreement.
course.s7.title: S7 — Mission states and interpretation
course.s7.body: S7 combines illumination, battery, usable RF and DSN overlap into operational, communications-only, survival, dark or unknown states. It totals useful hours and builds windows. Compare those outputs with your goals and coverage notes; totals need not form one uninterrupted interval.
course.s7.example: 1,200 unknown RF hours can lead to more unknown battery hours: once an earlier unknown load breaks the trajectory, later charge is still unknown.
course.s7.question: What do 216 confirmed useful hours prove?
course.s7.a: That the mission survives the entire evaluated year.
course.s7.c: That those sampled hours meet the model's useful-operation rules.
course.s7.explanation: Check blackout and unknown intervals separately. Tests, sourced equations and model comparisons support specific claims, not blanket physical qualification of S0–S7.
lessons.retry: Not yet. Review the explanation and try again.
lessons.practice: Compare two sites or dates in the Planner, then inspect power, radio windows and unknown intervals before exporting the report.
lessons.horizon.title: Sun, Earth and terrain
lessons.horizon.body: The Moon has no atmospheric refraction. The local terrain and lunar curvature determine the horizon. Sunlight and direct-to-Earth visibility are separate conditions: a ridge can hide Earth while a solar array remains illuminated.
lessons.horizon.question: The Sun is visible but Earth is hidden by terrain. What can you conclude?
lessons.horizon.b: Solar generation may be possible, but a direct geometric Earth line of sight is unavailable.
lessons.horizon.c: Both solar generation and communications must be zero.
lessons.horizon.explanation: Power also depends on panel orientation and visible solar-disc fraction. Terrain-obstructed radio propagation requires a separate link analysis; geometric blockage is not automatically a numerical RF margin.
lessons.energy.title: Power and battery
lessons.energy.body: RAVEN scales sunlight by distance, array area, efficiency, incidence and visible solar-disc fraction. Battery charge includes conversion losses and the selected loads. Generation is sampled at the start of a step; SOC is reported at its end. Panel, battery and load settings are illustrative, without a thermal or dust model.
lessons.energy.question: Why does a sunlight window alone not establish battery endurance?
lessons.energy.a: Orientation, load, capacity, losses and partially hidden sunlight also matter.
lessons.energy.c: Every visible Sun position produces identical power.
lessons.energy.explanation: Energy is power integrated over time, not just hours of sunlight. The discrete energy arithmetic has analytic checks; that is not physical validation of a real lunar power system.
lessons.energy.tool: Inspect energy settings in the Planner
lessons.radio.title: Radio windows and margin
lessons.radio.body: Earth visibility alone does not guarantee a radio link: antenna gain, pointing, diffraction, noise and bitrate affect margin, and DSN visibility is a separate constraint. Rounded-ridge and coherent multipath corrections have declared unvalidated assumptions. The wave tool is an educational view, not a lunar measurement.
lessons.radio.question: What does increasing compensator k change?
lessons.radio.a: It improves the physical margin at the same bitrate.
lessons.radio.c: It makes the selected bitrate more conservative, without changing fixed-rate physical margin.
lessons.radio.explanation: k expresses a statistical scheduling policy, not extra transmit power. Inspect the chosen-rate and margin graphs separately. Absolute lunar RF validation still needs a complete independent link budget.
lessons.evidence.title: Evidence and unknowns
lessons.evidence.body: V means sourced, D means derived and I means illustrative; these tags are not a certificate of physical validation. Formula checks, agreement between Python and browser code, and independent observations are different evidence. Missing terrain or upstream data remain unknown, including later battery states.
lessons.evidence.question: A candidate site has no terrain data. How should its result be interpreted?
lessons.evidence.a: Assume flat terrain and rank it normally.
lessons.evidence.b: Keep terrain-dependent quantities unknown and disclose the missing evidence.
lessons.evidence.c: Set all unknown values to zero.
lessons.evidence.explanation: Unknown is not false or zero. SOC and harvested-energy summaries cover the known prefix only; unknown intervals cannot establish mission feasibility. The validation matrix states what each check actually supports.

learn.phase.0: Phase 0 asks why the mission exists: who needs it, what it must achieve and how success will be recognised. It is a statement of need, not yet a design.
learn.phase.A: Phase A checks whether the idea is feasible: technically, in cost and in risk. Here RAVEN contributes its own results, such as sunlight and radio availability at the chosen sites.
learn.phase.B: Phase B defines the system at a preliminary level: the architecture, the main parts of the spacecraft and ground, the power and mass budgets and how each requirement will be verified.
learn.phase.C: Phase C turns the preliminary definition into a detailed design: components, drawings, software baselines and the plan for assembly, integration and test.
learn.phase.D: Phase D builds, integrates and tests the hardware and software until it is qualified and accepted for flight. RAVEN does not produce any evidence for this phase.
learn.phase.E: Phase E covers launch, commissioning and operations. RAVEN only describes the evaluated window and the operating conditions it computed; launch and ground booking are not planned here.
learn.phase.F: Phase F closes the mission: disposal, passivation, data close-out and the environmental and social footprint left behind.

sim.ui.learn: The lander, the ridge in front of it and the low Earth. Move the controls to update the scene, indicator, chart and map.
sim.ui.useRealHint: Only sites covered by a LOLA DEM are available. The scene and margin come from the engine; the controls adjust the antenna, data rate and time.
sim.ui.el: How high is Earth in the sky?
sim.ui.tip.el: Elevation: how many degrees Earth is above the horizon. At the south pole it is always low—only a few degrees.
sim.ui.tip.ridge: The ridge is the terrain between the lander and Earth. If it blocks Earth, the signal bends around the crest (diffraction).
sim.ui.tip.radius: A rounded crest bends the signal slightly less effectively than a sharp edge (ITU-R P.526-9 formula; not measured).
sim.ui.tip.dia: A larger antenna collects more signal, but its beam is narrower and must be pointed more accurately.
sim.ui.tip.rate: A higher data rate needs more signal: multiplying the rate by 10 costs 10 dB of margin.
sim.ui.tip.margin: Link margin is the signal remaining above the minimum. Above 0 dB the link closes. A 10 dB increase means ten times the power.
sim.ui.tip.fresnel: The Fresnel zone is the tube around the line of sight that the signal actually occupies. If the ridge intrudes into it, the signal weakens.
sim.ui.adv.realOnly: For a real site, the ridge, distance and radius come from terrain. Here you can adjust the antenna, mast, station, data rate and time.

lander.advancedIntro: At the south pole, Earth is only a few degrees above the horizon. The rover antenna points almost along the ground, and the ridge can cut into the first Fresnel zone (the translucent tube). Green, amber or red shows the link state calculated by the RAVEN engine; the text and numbers convey the same result.

lander.introSimple: The tube from the antenna is the signal path to Earth. If the ridge touches it, the signal weakens; if it blocks too much, the signal does not arrive. The colour and text explain the result.

wave.title: 3D wave
wave.introTitle: The wave beyond the ridge: why intensity oscillates
wave.learn: How the radio wave behaves just beyond the ridge: lower down it is in shadow and fades smoothly; above, it oscillates. A higher surface means a stronger signal.
wave.introSimple: A radio signal is a wave: when it grazes a ridge, it bends slightly downward (diffraction). That is why the region behind the ridge is a fading shadow, not a sharp dark boundary.
wave.introAdvanced: A plane wave grazing a ridge does not stop at a sharp line: beyond the edge, intensity falls smoothly in the shadow and oscillates above the line of sight (Fresnel fringes). The surface shows relative intensity |E|² versus distance from the ridge and height. Move the cursor to slice the surface and compare it with the exact knife-edge result.

wave.noSamplingWarnings: No sampling warnings for these parameters.
wave.figureDescription: Each surface point is field intensity |E|² divided by the free-wave intensity far from the ridge. At 1, the wave passes as if the ridge were absent; below 1, the ridge weakens it; above 1, a Fresnel fringe strengthens it.
wave.oscillationDescription: Different path lengths contribute beyond the edge: above the line of sight, the direct and diffracted waves alternately add in phase and cancel. Fringes widen farther from the ridge and at longer wavelengths (scale √(λx)); in the shadow, intensity fades without oscillating.
wave.nuSign: The ν parameter and its sign
wave.nuDescription: ν = −y·√(2/(λx)), where y is height above the line of sight (the ridge crest is y = 0) and x is distance. ν > 0 is the shadow (y < 0); ν < 0 is the illuminated region. The exact knife-edge result is |F(ν)|² using Fresnel integrals, shown as the dashed curve.
